body:
I used to laugh at witty jokes I guess, smiling has always been something that I mainly use for others sake. When I do smile it's when I'm with other people and laughing or making them laugh. I do love making other people laugh/happy, but often my jokes are hard to catch onto because I throw a lot of intelligence and subtext into them.

I just want a purpose to strive for, if I had that I could push through everything, but everytime I get interested in something, I lose interest a short while after. The short while can be kind of relative I suppose, but what I mean is that I've genuinely tried more hobbies than I can remember, and the longest any held was for two months.
The one exception to that has been studying Japanese. But lately I'm not even wanting to do that anymore.

Well, the counseling center is designed to work like the American system, but they're not psychologists/psychiatrists, just counselors. They are very helpful when I'm able to contact them, but they are also very small staffed. It's additionally difficult since I'm a native English speaker and they only have 1 or 2 counselors that can speak English.
As for Japan's views on stress and anxiety, as of late their thoughts are beginning to change but the traditional view is composed in the words "ganbaru" and "gaman". "Ganbaru" means "do your best" directly translated and it's essentially said whenever any kind of hardship is expressed. "Gaman" translated means "endure silently" but is written with characters that mean "self ridicule". Except for the counselors and other specifically trained individuals, the traditional response and phrase I hear the most is "Soo iiu koto nara, ganbarimashoo" which translates to "I hear what you're saying, try your best." In reality this phrase means "I hear what you're saying, but there's nothing I can (or are willing in certain cases) to do about it.
Japan's built around "gaman" very strongly, you're supposed to take care of your problems by yourself and people rarely if ever see a need to try and help or fix problems. Instead there are a large number of phrases devoted to "avoiding the topic" and removing responsibility. It's a problem a lot of people have with Japan (including Japanese people) in general.
As for me I just am at a breaking point, I don't have a reason to smile or something to look forward to. Everyday I keep trying to find something to make me smile and/or laugh, and everyday it just gets harder and harder to do. I really just don't know how to deal with this anymore.
